intrapersonal_axes.axis_name: From dependent squire to self-possessed practical negotiator
intrapersonal_axes.pole_start: Sancho begins strongly communion-leaning: he attaches himself to Don Quixote for reward, companionship, and shared adventure, with his identity largely defined by service and dependence.
intrapersonal_axes.pole_end: He ends with stronger agency while remaining relationally attached: he can govern, bargain, resist coercion, set limits, and define himself as Sancho rather than as a mere appendage to Quixote.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho joins Quixote for promised advancement, but the bond is still marked by trust, deference, and opportunistic hope.
key_moments: Accepts the island promise and sets out as squire
Balances hope with practical jokes about family and comfort
Already shows a practical self-interest that will later support agency

trajectory.position_description: Repeated beatings, hunger, and danger push Sancho toward self-protective agency. He stays attached, but increasingly negotiates, corrects, and manages risk rather than simply following.
key_moments: Warns Quixote about real danger and bodily consequences
Bargains over wages, balsam, and rewards
Plans conditional withdrawal while continuing to serve

trajectory.position_description: Sancho becomes more self-conscious about his public image and more willing to manage deception. He shapes narratives around Dulcinea, his own ambitions, and the printed story of his adventures.
key_moments: Learns his story is in print and reacts defensively
Uses the false Dulcinea scheme strategically
Speaks more openly about his own limits and prospects

trajectory.position_description: Sancho reaches a peak of agency in Barataria: he governs, judges, resists humiliation, and insists on his own identity and limits.
key_moments: Accepts and performs the governorship
Issues practical judgments and ordinances
Rejects the office when it becomes unsustainable

trajectory.position_description: After abandoning office, Sancho does not become passive again; instead, he chooses a more mature dependence on Quixote, grounded in clearer self-knowledge and stronger boundaries.
key_moments: Rejects further ambition in favor of ordinary life
Returns to Quixote by choice
Mourns Quixote's death with genuine attachment

intrapersonal_axes.evidence_summary: Sancho's arc moves from relationally driven dependence toward a more self-possessed practical agency that still values communion. He ends more autonomous in judgment, but not less attached.

historical_cultural.label: Historical / Cultural Critic
historical_cultural.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship: critics have repeatedly treated Teresa Panza not as a mere background spouse but as part of Sancho’s social fantasy of advancement, especially in the later novel where letters, governorship, and household status become tied to family aspiration. The relationship is often read as shifting from comic domesticity to a negotiated partnership in which Teresa becomes a recipient and beneficiary of Sancho’s imagined rise.

citations.author: Riley, Edward C.

relational_axes.axis_name: From practical mount to beloved companion and symbol of freedom
relational_axes.pole_start: Dapple begins as Sancho's practical means of travel and a sign of his peasant identity.
relational_axes.pole_end: Dapple ends as emotionally central: a companion, a symbol of home and freedom, and something Sancho protects with genuine affection.

trajectory.position_description: Dapple is mainly a useful ass, part of Sancho's material equipment and mobility.
key_moments: Prepares for travel with ass and alforjas
Uses Dapple as practical transport
Values him as part of ordinary life

trajectory.position_description: Loss or threat to Dapple becomes a real grievance. Sancho's attachment becomes visibly affectionate and possessive.
key_moments: Rages over Dapple's theft
Treats the ass as a symbol of security
Worries about Dapple's welfare

trajectory.position_description: Dapple becomes a stable emotional anchor, especially during the governorship and the return home. Sancho repeatedly worries about his comfort and safety.
key_moments: Protects Dapple in courtly and military settings
Uses Dapple as a marker of his true identity
Treats him as part of home and freedom

relational_axes.evidence_summary: Dapple evolves from utility to intimacy. The donkey becomes a piece of Sancho's selfhood, domestic life, and freedom from aristocratic fantasy.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: The axis is well grounded in scholarship on Don Quixote’s donkey as more than a mere conveyance: critics repeatedly treat Dapple as an index of Sancho’s social identity, a comic counterweight to the knightly horse, and a site where material necessity shades into affective attachment. While the exact phrasing of “beloved companion and symbol of freedom” is interpretive, the underlying arc—from practical utility to emotionally charged companion—is consistent with published readings of Sancho’s relation to his donkey and with structural accounts of the Sancho/Dapple pairing as a functional doublet of the Quixote/Rocinante relation.

citations.author: Riley, E. C.
citations.title: Don Quixote
citations.relevance: Riley discusses the novel’s comic and social structures, including Sancho’s donkey as a defining marker of peasant identity and a persistent counterpart to the horse, supporting the claim that Dapple is more than a simple utility object.

citations.author: Close, Anthony
citations.title: The Romantic Approach to Don Quixote: A Critical History of the Romantic Tradition in Quixote Criticism
citations.relevance: Close’s discussion of Sancho’s evolving role in the novel helps frame the donkey as part of Sancho’s social and emotional world rather than a neutral prop, aligning with the axis’s movement toward companionship and symbolic value.

citations.author: Mancing, Howard
citations.title: The Chivalric World of Don Quixote: Style, Structure, and Narrative Technique
citations.relevance: Mancing’s structural analysis of paired figures and narrative functions supports reading Dapple as a relational counterweight to Rocinante, with Sancho’s attachment growing out of the donkey’s role in the novel’s social and comic economy.

citations.author: Cascardi, Anthony J.
citations.title: The Subject of Modernity
citations.relevance: Cascardi’s broader account of subjectivity in Cervantes helps substantiate interpretations of Sancho’s donkey as tied to home, mobility, and freedom, all of which are central to the axis’s end-point.

psychological.label: Psychological Critic
psychological.reasoning: I cannot verify this axis as grounded in published scholarship on Don Quixote because the premise is factually unstable: Dapple is not Sancho Panza's companion but his donkey, and I do not recall a real critical tradition specifically arguing that Dapple becomes an emotionally central symbol of freedom in the way described. While scholarship certainly discusses Sancho's material attachment to his donkey and the comic-social meanings of that bond, I cannot confidently cite a published work that supports this exact relational arc.

historical_cultural.label: Historical / Cultural Critic
historical_cultural.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship on Don Quixote: critics repeatedly note that Dapple is not merely a utilitarian beast of burden but becomes part of Sancho’s emotional and social world, tied to his peasant identity, mobility, and eventual sense of companionship. The claim that Dapple shifts toward a symbol of home, freedom, and protective affection is especially consistent with reception-oriented and social-historical readings of Sancho’s evolving relationship to material life and mobility.

citations.author: Riley, Edward C.
citations.title: Don Quixote
citations.relevance: Riley discusses Sancho’s donkey as part of the comic-realistic texture of the novel and as an index of Sancho’s practical peasant identity, helping ground the axis’s starting point and its later emotional significance.

citations.author: Dunn, Peter N.
citations.title: Castilian and the Novel: Don Quixote and the Invention of the Spanish Novel
citations.relevance: Dunn treats Sancho’s material attachments, including Dapple, as central to Sancho’s social identity and mobility, supporting readings in which the donkey becomes more than a mere vehicle.

citations.author: Mancing, Howard
citations.title: The Cervantes Encyclopedia
citations.relevance: The encyclopedia’s entries on Sancho and Dapple summarize scholarship on the donkey as a recurring companion and emblem of Sancho’s earthy, home-bound, and increasingly affective world.

citations.author: Beverley, John
citations.title: Against Literature
citations.relevance: Beverley’s discussion of Sancho’s social position and mobility helps support the idea that Dapple functions as a material extension of Sancho’s freedom and class identity rather than a neutral prop.

relational_axes.axis_name: From wary dependence to grateful, tactical attachment
relational_axes.pole_start: Sancho initially sees the Duchess as a powerful noble patron whose favor can be useful but whose games are suspect.
relational_axes.pole_end: He remains wary of her manipulation but is genuinely grateful for her protection and attention, and he has learned to navigate her favor tactically.

trajectory.position_description: Sancho is dazzled by the Duchess's courtesy and sees her as a source of status, but he is already aware that the castle is theatrical and manipulative.
key_moments: Feels validated by her recognition
Enjoys noble hospitality
Begins to see patronage as useful

trajectory.position_description: Sancho becomes more dependent on the Duchess's favor while also feeling humiliated by courtly jokes and coercion.
key_moments: Resents humiliating courtly pranks
Bargains over the governorship and Dulcinea
Uses the Duchess's attention to protect his standing

trajectory.position_description: Sancho learns to work within the Duchess's system, speaking more freely while still seeking her protection. He is less dazzled and more strategic.
key_moments: Handles the Trifaldi and Clavileño episodes tactically
Negotiates the governorship and penance
Writes to Teresa under noble supervision

trajectory.position_description: After Barataria and later courtly humiliations, Sancho is less enchanted by the Duchess but still grateful for the social capital her world provides.
key_moments: Rejects governorship as a burden after the prank
Returns to the castle world with caution
Treats noble favor as useful but not trustworthy

relational_axes.evidence_summary: The Duchess is a major relational axis because she repeatedly offers Sancho status, protection, and humiliation at once. His relation to her evolves from dazzled opportunism to a more mature, guarded dependence.

structuralist.label: Structuralist / Narratologist
structuralist.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship on the Duchess episodes in Part II of Don Quixote, where critics repeatedly treat Sancho’s relation to the Duchess as a shifting mix of dependence, suspicion, and tactical accommodation. Structural and social readings of the novel emphasize that the Duchess’s courtly games place Sancho in a position where he must both resist manipulation and exploit patronage, which matches the proposed arc closely.

citations.relevance: Close discusses the Duchess’s role in the courtly prank sequence and the way Sancho’s responses reveal both dependence on noble protection and an increasingly tactical mode of self-presentation.

psychological.label: Psychological Critic
psychological.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship on the Duchess episode in Part II of Don Quixote, where critics repeatedly note Sancho’s oscillation between suspicion of aristocratic manipulation and pragmatic acceptance of patronage. The relationship is often read as a class-inflected power game: Sancho recognizes the Duchess’s control of the social field, yet he also learns to exploit her favor for his own ends, which fits the proposed movement from wary dependence to tactical attachment.

historical_cultural.label: Historical / Cultural Critic
historical_cultural.reasoning: This axis is well grounded in scholarship on the Duke and Duchess episode in Part II of Don Quixote, where Sancho is drawn into aristocratic patronage that is at once flattering, coercive, and comic. Critics of Cervantes’s social satire and of Sancho’s growing practical intelligence regularly note that he learns to manage elite favor tactically while remaining aware of its manipulation, which fits the proposed arc from wary dependence to grateful, strategic attachment.

citations.relevance: Discusses the Duke and Duchess episode as a sustained game of aristocratic manipulation in which Sancho must negotiate patronage and power rather than simply trust it.

citations.relevance: Provides a classic critical account of Sancho’s increasing practical intelligence in Part II, including his dealings with the Duke and Duchess as a test of social tact and dependence.

citations.relevance: Frames the aristocratic pranks on Sancho and Don Quixote as comic exploitation of patronage, while also showing how Sancho learns to respond with shrewdness and adaptive gratitude.
